q: A projectile is any object thrown into space upon which the only acting force is the gravity.
e: By definition, a projectile is an object acted upon solely by gravity after being thrown into space.

q: The path followed by a projectile is known as a displacement.
e: The path followed by a projectile is known as a trajectory.

q: The motion of an object moving in both horizontal x direction and vertical y direction simultaneously is called the projectile motion.
e: Projectile motion is characterized by simultaneous motion in both horizontal and vertical directions.

q: If air resistance is neglected, an object moves along the horizontal x direction with a constant acceleration.
e: If air resistance is neglected, an object moves along the horizontal x direction with a constant velocity, not acceleration.

q: If air resistance is neglected, an object moves in the vertical y direction with constant downward acceleration.
e: In the vertical direction, the object experiences a constant downward acceleration due to gravity.

q: In projectile motion with neglected air resistance, only gravitational force is acting on the object.
e: Gravity is the sole force acting on a projectile when air resistance is ignored.

q: The downward acceleration is the acceleration due to gravity $g$ which is a constant over the range of motion.
e: The acceleration due to gravity $g$ is treated as a constant throughout the projectile's range.

q: The vertical motion of a projectile is a uniform motion.
e: The vertical motion of a projectile is a free fall motion, not a uniform motion.

q: In the x direction of projectile motion, $a_x = 0$ and $v_x = v_0 \cos \theta = \text{constant}$.
e: There is no horizontal acceleration, so the horizontal velocity component remains constant.

q: The horizontal displacement of a projectile can be written as a function of time as $x = (v_0 \cos \theta) t$.
e: Since horizontal velocity is constant, horizontal displacement is simply velocity multiplied by time.

q: In the y direction of projectile motion, $v_{oy}$ is the initial velocity and $a_y$ is $-g$.
e: The initial vertical velocity is $v_{oy}$ and the acceleration is downward, hence $-g$.

q: The velocity of a projectile in the y direction in time $t$ is given by $v_y = v_{oy} + gt$.
e: The correct equation is $v_y = v_{oy} - gt$ because the acceleration due to gravity acts downward.

q: The displacement of a projectile in the y direction in time $t$ is given by $y = v_{oy} t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
e: This is the standard kinematic equation for vertical displacement under constant downward acceleration.

q: The magnitude of the velocity of the projectile at any instant of time is $v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$.
e: The total velocity magnitude is found using the Pythagorean theorem on its perpendicular components.

q: The direction of the velocity of the projectile is given by $\tan \theta = \frac{v_x}{v_y}$.
e: The direction is given by $\tan \theta = \frac{v_y}{v_x}$, the ratio of the vertical component to the horizontal component.

q: The projectile reaches the highest point when its horizontal component of velocity $v_x$ is zero.
e: The projectile reaches the highest point when its vertical component of velocity $v_y$ is zero.

q: The time taken to reach the highest point is $t_1 = \frac{v_0 \sin \theta}{g}$.
e: This is derived by setting the final vertical velocity $v_y$ to zero in the velocity-time equation.

q: The time of flight is equal to the time to reach the maximum height.
e: The time of flight is twice the time to reach the maximum height.

q: The time of flight of a projectile is $T = \frac{2 v_0 \sin \theta}{g}$.
e: The total time of flight is double the time taken to reach the peak of the trajectory.

q: The maximum height of the projectile is $H = \frac{(v_0 \cos \theta)^2}{2g}$.
e: The maximum height depends on the vertical component of velocity: $H = \frac{(v_0 \sin \theta)^2}{2g}$.

q: The horizontal range $R$ is the horizontal distance from the starting point to the point where the projectile returns to the same height.
e: This is the exact definition of horizontal range in projectile motion.

q: The horizontal range is obtained as $R = \frac{v_0^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$.
e: This formula is derived by substituting the time of flight into the horizontal displacement equation.

q: For an object thrown horizontally, there is a vertical component to its initial velocity.
e: For an object thrown horizontally, there is no vertical component to its initial velocity ($v_{oy} = 0$).

q: For an object thrown horizontally, the vertical velocity of the object in time $t$ is $v_y = -gt$.
e: Since initial vertical velocity is zero, the vertical velocity at time $t$ is solely due to gravitational acceleration.

q: For an object thrown horizontally, the vertical displacement in time $t$ is $y = -\frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
e: With zero initial vertical velocity, the vertical displacement follows the free fall equation.
